extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, litigators, scholars, and those who follow Federal Circuit precedent
extracted.subtask_description: A blog-post list and commentary identifying the most-cited Federal Circuit precedents in 2025, emphasizing claim-construction classics and recent procedural (threshold/reviewability) decisions that shape patent litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phillips v. AWH Corp. (claim construction framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms carry their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention, with that meaning informed primarily by the intrinsic record: i.e., the claims, the specification, and the prosecution history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phillips (en banc) is described as the undisputed foundation of claim construction doctrine and leads citation counts in 2025. The decision resolved tension about the relative weight of intrinsic versus extrinsic evidence, subordinating dictionaries and expert testimony to the patent document itself. (Data based on parsing CAFC's 2025 precedential patent decisions through December 15, 2025.)

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR v. Teleflex (obviousness standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: KSR v. Teleflex appears among the most frequently cited precedents and represents the Federal Circuit's treatment of the obviousness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes KSR as the second-most-cited precedent in 2025, indicating that obviousness doctrine remains a frequently-invoked substantive standard on the court's docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markman v. Westview (claim construction allocation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Markman is listed among the top-cited cases and is one of the 'claim construction classics' appearing in the compilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Markman's inclusion signals continued reliance on precedents establishing how claim construction is treated (i.e., the allocation of claim interpretation to the court). The post does not elaborate further but lists Markman as a staple authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cuozzo v. Lee (IPR judicial reviewability precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cuozzo v. Lee is cited as one of two cases on the list that address inter partes review (IPR) judicial reviewability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post highlights Cuozzo as part of the court's post-AIA docket focus; its presence among the most-cited opinions reflects disputes over whether and how PTO/PTAB decisions in IPRs are subject to judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thryv v. Click‑To‑Call (IPR judicial reviewability precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thryv v. Click‑To‑Call is similarly noted as addressing IPR judicial reviewability and is among the top ten cited precedents in 2025.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Along with Cuozzo, Thryv's citation frequency underscores the prominence of post-AIA procedural issues (reviewability of PTAB decisions) in Federal Circuit opinions for 2025.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidated Edison Co. v. NLRB (appellate-review boundary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consolidated Edison Co. v. NLRB (1938) — the oldest case on the list — is said to define the boundary of appellate review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Its inclusion shows that longstanding administrative-law principles about the scope and limits of appellate review remain relevant to patent appeals and are still cited in 2025.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural threshold issues (preservation, standard of review, availability of judicial review)
rubrics_metrics.description: The post emphasizes the prominence of procedural cases addressing threshold questions: whether arguments were preserved, what standard of review applies, and whether judicial review is even available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'procedural turn' is identified as a notable feature of the 2025 citation data: many of the most-cited precedents are not only substantive doctrines but also procedural standards that determine if and how issues reach appellate review (preservation rules, deference/standard of review, and statutory/constitutional limits on reviewability).
